source.title: Breaking Data Symmetry is Needed For Generalization in Feature Learning Kernels
source.authors: Marcelo Bernal; Neil Rohit Mallinar; Mikhail Belkin

page_placements.theme: Task structure, encoding and sampling govern learnability

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that RFM generalization on algebraic tasks can depend strongly on whether the training partition preserves a symmetry, refining the account of when grokking-like generalization occurs.
record.gate_note: The study also discusses prior grokking results, which are not recorded as its own findings. It does not report training-accuracy curves or a comparison of optimization delay across training-set sizes. Results described only qualitatively from plots are recorded as figure-only where applicable.
record.test_reason: The study frames itself around grokking but never measures delayed generalization. It trains RFM kernels for a fixed 60 iterations and reports final test accuracy as a function of train-test partition symmetry. The x-axes in Figures 1 and 5–7 are the number of points moved, not training iterations. It reports no training-accuracy saturation, no time to generalize, and no delay versus training-set size. So its rows cannot show V1's effect (a late jump whose delay grows as data shrinks), and no other version is touched. Its finding, that RFM generalizes only when the partition breaks a reflection symmetry, concerns a different question: whether generalization happens at all. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The reader's T5/tests classification is not supported: the authors do not argue that V1 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that RFM generalizes on Abelian-group addition tasks only when the training partition breaks invariance under a subgroup of the target's symmetry group. They find that learned AGOP features encode the corresponding group elements, and that subgroup-encoding initializations restrict generalization to the training set's orbit. They state that data symmetry alone suffices to explain RFM's generalization behaviour here, while noting that H-invariance is not the full picture: imposing feature structure can also restore generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses recursive feature machines with Gaussian and quadratic feature-learning kernels, rather than reproducing the original neural-network training method. It focuses on the effect of algebraic data partitions and symmetry.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with whether the training partition preserves a symmetry, how many random points are moved, the kernel, and the subgroup encoded in the initial feature matrix.

fits_no_version.finding: RFM (Gaussian and quadratic kernels) reaches 0% test accuracy when the held-out set is the fixed points of a reflection. Moving random training points to the test set restores up to 97–98% accuracy; moving symmetric pairs or fixed points does not (Table 1; Figures 1, 5–8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On algebraic tasks, whether a feature-learning model generalizes depends on whether the train partition is invariant under a subgroup of the target's symmetry group, not just on the training fraction.

fits_no_version.finding: With the initial feature matrix encoding a reflection subgroup and a random 50% split, the correctly classified test points exactly match the training set's orbit under that subgroup (100% precision and recall; Figures 4, 15, 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For RFM, an initialization encoding a subgroup restricts generalization to the training set's orbit under that subgroup.

fits_no_version.finding: Holding out one point (about 99% training fraction) prevents generalization. Holding out two points generalizes only if they are not fixed under a common reflection (Section 3; Figure 5B). Initializing with a different reflection recovers 100% accuracy on a fixed-point test set (Discussion; Appendix F, Figure 14). No rows record these.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Symmetry traps in RFM can be escaped by breaking data symmetry or by imposing a different feature prior.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2026), PMLR Volume 300
record.problems: The study does not measure training accuracy or optimization-time delays, so it cannot establish a long delay after training accuracy saturates or compare delay across training-set sizes. Many additional outcomes are presented qualitatively in plots without numeric accuracies or uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Training-accuracy saturation, a delayed test-accuracy jump over training iterations, and how the delay scales with training-set size. Only final accuracy after 60 RFM iterations is reported.
No progress measures over iterations. The AGOP feature structure is shown only at the final iteration.
Not tested: algebraic tasks only, and no initialization-scale or lazy/rich manipulation.
Not tested: no weight decay, norm, or critical-dataset-size analysis.
Not tested: there is no cross-run or cross-architecture algorithm comparison.

missing.what: Single-point and two-point hold-out results (about 99% training fraction fails to generalize)
missing.locator: Section 3 paragraph before Finding 3.1; Appendix D.1, Figure 5B

missing.what: Initializing M0 with a different reflection recovers 100% accuracy on the fixed-point test set; Figure 14 B–D orbit-removal results

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T5 and V1 limits_scope label are withdrawn. No measure tracks generalization over training time, so V1's delay claim cannot be assessed. The less-data-generalizes-better result concerns final generalization, not delay length. Figure 1's caption (p=53) conflicts with the text, which attributes the same 98% result to p=61.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests generalization on algorithmic tasks under different data partitions, but does not measure training-accuracy saturation, a delayed test-accuracy jump over optimization time, or whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

relation.reason: Grokking motivates the study and informs its discussion, but its own reported results concern partition symmetry and final generalization rather than the claimed delay or its dynamics.

tranche.reason: The study measures final generalization under partition and feature-initialization interventions, without measuring delayed generalization or testing another claim version. Its plotted intervention axes count moved samples, not training iterations.

source_check.notes: Figure 1's caption specifies p=53 while its accompanying discussion specifies p=61; r13 accurately flags this conflict. The symmetry requirement is conditional: Section 6 and Appendix F show that a different encoded reflection at initialization restores 100% accuracy without breaking partition symmetry.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Symmetry-invariant fixed-point partitions and symmetric-pair moves
reader_labels.reason: RFM fails to generalize on these partitions, while breaking the partition symmetry can restore generalization; this makes the outcome conditional on the data partition (r2, r4, r7, r10, r13, r16, r19-r22).
